theory.title: Academic Register and Disciplinary Discourse
theory.explanation: This mission develops advanced academic register. Effective C2 communication requires writers and speakers to make purpose, audience, evidence and degree of certainty explicit. Analyse the context before choosing a register; distinguish established information from interpretation; organise complex material so that decisions and qualifications remain visible.
theory.tip: Use precise terminology, attribute claims, qualify uncertainty and make the requested action explicit.

patterns.label: Define purpose and audience
patterns.pattern: Identify what the audience needs to know or decide.
examples: State the decision required before presenting supporting detail.

patterns.label: Support and qualify
patterns.pattern: Connect each claim to evidence and state relevant limitations.
examples: The findings suggest a pattern, although the sample is not representative.

patterns.label: Structure for action
patterns.pattern: Use signposting, headings and explicit ownership.
examples: The recommendation is assigned to a named lead for review by an agreed date.

patterns.label: Review for integrity
patterns.pattern: Check terminology, attribution, tone and consistency.
examples: Distinguish verified outcomes from projected benefits.

content.passage:
A research group preparing a report for both historians and data scientists discovered that the same term carried different assumptions in each field. The historians used 'evidence' to include archival context and provenance; the data scientists used it more narrowly for observations that could be operationalised. Rather than flattening the distinction, the editor added a short definition and attributed each claim to the relevant discipline.

The revised report also reduced unnecessary nominalisations. Where the draft had stated that 'an evaluation of the reliability of the records was undertaken', the final version said that 'the team evaluated the records' reliability'. This change made the agent and action visible without sacrificing formality. Cautious language was retained where the sample was limited, but removed where the evidence was direct.

The final text did not aim to sound uniformly formal. It aimed to make its stance legible, its terminology consistent and its degree of certainty proportionate to the evidence. The editor concluded that academic register is not a decorative layer: it is a set of choices that helps readers distinguish findings, interpretations and unresolved questions.
